name: PT Batulicin Nusantara Maritim Tbk

frontmatter.title: Batulicin Nusantara Maritim: a two-customer coal barge fleet priced for a recovery that has not started
frontmatter.summary: BESS is a South Kalimantan tug-and-barge transhipment operator whose revenue collapsed in the first half of 2026 as its two anchor coal miners cut volumes, leaving a fixed cost base and a small loss. The shares still trade on peak-cycle earnings and book. We initiate at SELL.
thesis: H1-2026 revenue fell sharply and the group swung to a pre-tax loss; the fixed cost base (depreciation, crew, inspection, barge rent) did not flex.
Two customers supplied almost all FY2025 revenue, so the volume loss is company-specific and cannot be read as a market cycle alone.
The FY2026 budget is already unreachable; our base case puts FY2026 revenue well below it and recovers only part of the gap by FY2027.
{'The price discounts a full recovery and more': 'the reverse DCF needs FY2027 growth far above our base case.'}
Net cash and a small dividend support the floor, but not the current valuation.

catalysts.event: Q3-2026 financial statements: the first read on whether the H1 volume trough persisted
Coal price and ICI assessments; customer offtake and nickel transhipment news
FY2026 audited results and the FY2027 budget
AGM and the dividend decision on FY2026 profit

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Batulicin Nusantara Maritim Tbk at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp185**, implying a total return of **-74.0%** from the Rp710 close [S0]. The target is the probability-weighted scenario value after the house liquidity discount, built on a through-cycle FCFF DCF at a WACC of 12.5% and an asset-backed P/B cross-check.

The variant view is that the market is still capitalising the FY2025 peak, not the business as it now runs. FY2025 revenue was IDR353.7bn and net profit IDR63.6bn [S3], and the shares still trade on 38.4x trailing earnings and 3.7x book [S0]. But in H1-2026 revenue fell to IDR110.4bn and the group booked a pre-tax loss of IDR5.6bn [S2]. The cost base is largely fixed — depreciation alone was IDR39.5bn in FY2025 [S3] — so a volume shortfall goes almost straight to the margin.

Three things move the value. First, whether the two anchor miners restore volumes: they supplied almost all FY2025 revenue, with PT Tanah Bumbu Resources at IDR297.4bn and PT Sungai Danau Jaya at IDR53.3bn [S3]. Second, the fuel spread: bunker fuel was IDR55.9bn of FY2025 cost of revenue and is only partly passed through [S3]. Third, third-party barge rent, which more than doubled in the first half of 2026 versus the prior-year half as owned capacity was supplemented [S2].

The balance sheet is a genuine support: the group is in net cash and the bank facility is small [S2]. The dividend is modest — IDR15.0bn declared from FY2025 profit and still payable at the half-year [S2]. None of that bridges the gap to the current price.

Our base case is the most probable path, not the safest one. We assume the FY2026 trough is real, only a partial recovery in FY2027, and a long-run margin below the FY2025 peak because the cheap barge rent that flattered FY2025 is already normalising [S2, S3]. The consequence is honest: FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is negative on the working-capital and capex resets, and the rating does not depend on the arithmetic being conservative — it depends on the market still capitalising the peak.

Coal transhipment is a narrow-margin, asset-heavy link in the Indonesian export chain: shallow-draft barges load at a river or jetty and transfer cargo to ocean-going vessels at an anchorage. Returns depend on tonnes moved, distance and waiting time, and the spread between the freight tariff and the cost of fuel, crew and vessel upkeep. Because a barge fleet is fixed in the short run, a fall in one customer's offtake hits utilisation quickly. This is general industry context, not a company fact.

BESS provides domestic tramper sea freight for goods — in practice coal and, increasingly, nickel — using its own tugboats and barges, and tranships cargo to mother vessels [S3]. The company is based at Batulicin in Tanah Bumbu, South Kalimantan, close to the mines and private jetties it serves [S3]. Revenue is recognised when the freight service is delivered, and the LK describes a single service line rather than reportable segments [S3].

The customer base is the defining feature. In FY2025 two miners accounted for nearly all revenue: PT Tanah Bumbu Resources at IDR297.4bn and PT Sungai Danau Jaya at IDR53.3bn, with a third customer at a token amount [S3]. In H1-2026 the same two names still dominated, with Sungai Danau Jaya down to IDR14.5bn [S2]. The LK and the annual report disclose no take-or-pay commitment to either customer; tariffs and volumes are described as negotiated [S3, S4].

The group is controlled through PT Batulicin Enam Sembilan Transportasi, which holds 78.4% of the shares, with PT Batulicin Enam Sembilan as ultimate parent [S4]. The disclosed ultimate beneficial owners are Sitti Mariani, Mardani H. Maming and Rois Sunandar, described as an organised group [S4]. The parent provides management services for a fee of IDR2.9bn a year [S3], and related parties also supply fuel, security and barge capacity [S3].

Operations are capital-intensive, and the fleet is supplemented with chartered tonnage at peaks: the company says it may charter third-party vessels when demand is high [S4]. In H1-2026 barge rent rose to IDR11.7bn against IDR13.0bn for the whole of FY2025, consistent with heavier reliance on hired capacity as owned utilisation fell [S2, S3].

The fleet itself is the operating asset: tugs and barges are deployed on coal routes and, increasingly, nickel transhipment, so utilisation rather than the headline tariff is the swing factor in a year [S3, S4]. Strategy is to deepen the two anchor relationships while adding nickel cargo and keeping the balance sheet in net cash; no large fleet expansion or acquisition is disclosed [S3, S4]. Within the single service line, coal transhipment dominates and nickel is a small but growing contributor; the LK does not break revenue by commodity, so the mix has to be inferred from the customer note and management commentary [S3, S4].

Market position is that of a regional challenger rather than a national leader. The company competes on jetty access, proximity and reliability rather than scale, and its revenue is a function of two mines rather than of national coal volumes [S3, S4]. Because a single customer can move cargo to a rival barge owner, there is no contractual lock-in disclosed that would protect the franchise through a volume cycle [S3]. Coal movements at a river jetty are also exposed to weather, tide and anchorage congestion; the LK does not split revenue by quarter, but the FY2026 half-year swing shows how quickly the top line can move [S2].

Indonesian coal output was 790 Mt Mt in 2025, down from the prior year, with exports the majority of the mix and the Domestic Market Obligation at 254 Mt Mt [S4]. The company's own review notes that ICI 4 prices fell 20.0% in the first half of 2025 before a modest second-half recovery [S4]. Our coal deck carries a Newcastle marker of US$118/t a tonne for FY2027E and a long-run marker of US$105/t, against a spot print of US$150/t — the war-premium carry that the desk does not expect to persist (house coal deck, reviewed).

The export pool is the market that matters: domestic burn is administered through the DMO, so the addressable transhipment volume is the export share, which moves with Chinese and Indian demand and with the price spread between Indonesian and Australian coal [S4]. Regulation sits upstream of BESS rather than on it: mining permits, the DMO and the royalty regime determine how much coal its customers move, while cabotage and port rules govern the barges themselves [S4].

For a barge operator the coal price matters through two channels: miners' willingness to move tonnes, and the barge and sub-charter rates that clear the marginal cargo. The company attributes its FY2025 revenue beat to extra customer demand and higher ICI in the second half [S4]. The 2026 coal tape has been strong, yet BESS's volumes fell — evidence that its problem is customer-specific, not a collapse in the coal market [S2, S4].

Demand for transhipment is also being fed by nickel. The annual report cites national nickel output and smelter build-out as a new pool of cargo, and management is steering the fleet toward coal and nickel transhipment [S4]. That is a real diversification opportunity but, on the disclosed numbers, not yet large enough to offset the coal volume loss [S2]. The LK does not split nickel revenue or volumes, so we do not put a nickel value in the base case: we carry it as a sourced free option, the natural offset to a customer-specific coal loss and a contributor to the bull scenario [S4].

Competitive position is modest. BESS is a small regional operator, not a national leader; its edge is proximity to the Tanah Bumbu mines and jetty access, and its weakness is customer concentration and a fleet that must be supplemented with hired barges [S3, S4]. Barriers to entry are capital and permits rather than technology, so pricing power is limited when a customer can switch operator. On the five forces: buyer power is high with two customers, supplier power is moderate because fuel and chartered barges come partly from related parties, rivalry is local and rate-driven, substitutes are trucking and alternative jetties, and new entry is possible for well-capitalised operators [S3, S4]. The moat is thin: proximity and jetty access are real but local, they do not stop a miner from contracting a rival barge owner or building its own loading facility, and switching costs are low because the service is standardised [S3, S4]. The company's own use of chartered tonnage shows that capacity can be bought in the market, which is why we treat the franchise as cyclical rather than defensive [S3].

External influences cut both ways. A weaker rupiah raises the IDR value of dollar-linked coal revenue but also the cost of imported fuel, lubricants and spare parts, so the net effect on a barge operator's spread is ambiguous [S3]. Our deck assumes continued rupiah depreciation against the dollar, which supports the rupiah revenue line but not the margin [S3]. No market share is published; the company is small relative to the national barge fleet, and its revenue tracks two mines rather than national volumes [S3, S4].

Indonesian domestic shipping is protected by cabotage rules, which reserve domestic sea transport to Indonesian-flagged and Indonesian-owned vessels. That supports local operators against foreign competition but does not protect them from a customer moving cargo to a rival domestic barge owner or to a different jetty. Port and transhipment economics also depend on draft, tide and anchorage congestion, which vary by location. This is general industry context, not a company fact.

Revenue ran at IDR363.7bn, IDR318.9bn and IDR353.7bn over the last three fiscal years, with gross margin moving from 35.6% to 31.0% and then 37.3% [S0, S3]. The FY2025 improvement was flattered by unusually cheap third-party barge rent — IDR13.0bn against a much higher level in FY2024 — and by demurrage income [S3].

The data pack materially understates depreciation: it carries a token charge, while the LK shows IDR39.5bn of depreciation in FY2025 and IDR39.5bn in FY2023 [S3, S6]. We restate D&A, operating expenses and EBIT from the LK, which lifts FY2025 EBITDA to IDR118.3bn against the pack's figure [S3]. The engine rebuilds history from those facts; readers should treat the restated EBITDA, not the pack, as the base.

FY2025 net profit of IDR63.6bn came after a IDR15.2bn impairment of trade receivables [S3]. That is a real credit cost, not an accounting nuisance: it equals a meaningful share of revenue and follows a smaller charge in FY2024 [S3]. H1-2026 carried only a small impairment, but the operating loss was the larger issue [S2].

Tax is not the statutory corporate rate. Domestic tramper sea freight is subject to final Article 15 tax at 1.2% of gross revenue — IDR4.2bn in FY2025 — so the group pays tax on revenue even when it makes a loss [S3]. We set the forecast tax charge to reproduce that fixed revenue-based burden at each year's profit, so the rate falls as margins recover. The engine's tax line cannot levy a charge in a loss year, a known limitation we flag to OPS; FY2026E cash tax is understated by roughly the final-tax charge on that year's revenue.

Cost of revenue is dominated by fuel, depreciation, inspection and maintenance, and barge rent [S3]. Depreciation inside cost of revenue was IDR39.0bn in FY2025, and docking and inspection are expensed rather than capitalised, which is why reported capex is so low [S3]. The structure means the gross margin is highly geared to volume: a shortfall spreads the same fixed charges over fewer tonnes, and no tariff increase can offset that within a year [S2].

The H1-2026 collapse is the central fact. Revenue fell to IDR110.4bn, cost of revenue was IDR92.3bn, gross profit IDR18.1bn and the pre-tax result a loss of IDR5.6bn [S2]. Fuel cost fell with volume to IDR20.5bn, but depreciation, crew, inspection and permits did not [S2]. The company's FY2026 budget, set before the downturn, assumed revenue of IDR372.0bn and pre-tax profit of IDR60.3bn [S4]; the first half has already made that unreachable, and we model FY2026 revenue far below it.

Our forecast has FY2026 revenue of IDR220.7bn, gross margin of 16.8%, an operating loss of IDR-10.3bn and EBITDA of IDR27.2bn. FY2027 recovers to IDR256.0bn of revenue and IDR56.2bn of EBITDA as volumes partially return, still below FY2025. By FY2028 the group is back to IDR72.2bn of EBITDA, and long-run margins settle near the FY2023-FY2025 average once barge rent normalises [S3].

FY2025 cash conversion was strong, but it did not repeat. H1-2026 operating cash flow was negative [S2], and trade receivables were IDR68.8bn at the half-year, barely changed from the December level while revenue collapsed [S2]. We therefore hold operating working capital at the latest actual ratio rather than assume the cash release that a falling revenue line would normally create; FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is negative, consistent with the H1 cash burn [S2]. Capital expenditure is tiny in the accounts — well under D&A — because dry-docking and repairs are expensed; we normalise capex to half the D&A charge to fund eventual fleet replacement, a drag on free cash flow that the reported numbers hide [S3].

Net debt is negative. The group held IDR184.8bn of cash at the FY2025 year-end against a small amortising facility, and net cash stays positive through the trough even though the cash balance falls in FY2026E as working capital absorbs funds [S2, S3]. Capital allocation is conservative: no material acquisition, no rights issue, and no dividend in the loss year [S2, S4]. The two lines to watch are receivables and the impairment charge, because a single customer's delay moves both [S3].

The earnings-quality screen flags three things. Customer concentration is extreme and rising: PT Tanah Bumbu Resources supplied IDR297.4bn of FY2025 revenue [S3]. Related-party gravity is structural: purchases from companies under common control were IDR53.2bn in cost of revenue — 24.0% of the total — and IDR7.6bn in operating expenses, including the parent's management fee [S3]. And the FY2025 impairment shows receivables can go bad quickly when a miner's cash flow turns [S3]. We found no evidence of special-monitoring-board status or notation letters in the documents reviewed; the shares are simply very tightly held.

We value BESS on a through-cycle FCFF DCF, cross-checked against P/B. This fits a coal-logistics business because earnings are cyclical and asset-backed: the fleet, the customer relationships and the net cash position are what a buyer owns, and a single-year multiple on trough or peak EBITDA misleads. We carry the DCF at 70% and P/B at 30% of the blend. We have zero-weighted the house EV/EBITDA cross-check: the engine applies the peer-median multiple to last-actual (FY2025A) EBITDA, which is above mid-cycle, and the commodity-cyclical card forbids a current-year multiple for cyclicals. The comparable bargers in the peer set — BBRM, DWGL and MAHA — trade on mid-single-digit EV/EBITDA, while the peer median is lifted by two small high-multiple names; applied to FY2025A EBITDA the method would add value the DCF does not support, so it is displayed but contributes nothing.

The DCF discounts nominal rupiah cash flows at a WACC of 12.5%, built from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, an equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5% and an unlevered beta of 1.00, with almost no net debt. The rupiah cost of equity is net of the Indonesia sovereign default spread of 1.6% embedded in the deck's risk-free rate; adding the components without that deduction overstates the hurdle. Terminal growth is 3.0%, below the house default because Indonesian thermal-coal volumes are in structural decline [S4]. The DCF produces Rp183 a share, with the terminal value 46.7% of the total — moderate for a ten-year model.

P/B gives Rp219 at 1.2 times book, 19.7% versus the DCF, the more defensible cross-check for an asset-backed operator with net cash at a cyclical trough. The DCF is the primary because the book value is not a claim on cash flow: the H1-2026 volume loss is exactly what the asset base has to earn through, and a P/B that ignores the earnings power of that fleet overstates the floor [S2].

The peer set is imperfect by construction: there are few listed Indonesian barge operators of comparable size, so the P/B multiple is drawn from a broader marine group and used only as a cross-check. For an asset-backed, net-cash business the P/B anchor is informative, which is why it carries weight above its house share. We also tested a no-recovery case: if FY2027 volumes stay at the H1-2026 run-rate, the DCF falls toward the bear scenario, so the downside is a cash-flow outcome rather than only a multiple de-rating [S2]. The terminal value rests on the long-run coal marker and a modest growth rate; a lower terminal coal price would cut value materially [S4].

On the dividend anchor the commodity card asks for: BESS is not priced off dividend capacity. At the modelled payout the DPS is Rp1, a yield far below the risk-free rate of 7.4%; even if the payout were doubled, the yield would remain below the risk-free rate. The model leaves net cash rising because the FCFE is retained, not distributed [S3]. The market is therefore using an NAV anchor, not a dividend anchor, and our call is that the NAV is lower than the price.

The probability-weighted value is Rp231; after the house liquidity discount of 20.0% — the shares turn over only IDR197.7m a day and the free float is 15.4% [S0] — the target is Rp185. The reverse DCF is the cleanest statement of the gap: at today's price the market implies FY2027 revenue growth of 42.8%, against 16.0% in our base case. That is a recovery beyond anything the first half supports.

The largest downside is customer concentration. PT Tanah Bumbu Resources alone supplied IDR297.4bn of FY2025 revenue, and both anchor miners cut volumes in H1-2026 [S2, S3]; losing or insourcing that customer, or a further step-down in offtake, would leave the fixed cost base stranded. Likelihood high, impact high.

Coal price and volume risk is next. A weaker Newcastle/ICI tape would reduce miners' willingness to move marginal tonnes and pressure barge rates; the deck's long-run marker is far below spot (house coal deck, reviewed) [S4]. Likelihood medium, impact high.

Fuel is a margin risk: bunker cost is one of the largest lines in cost of revenue and pass-through is partial [S3]. A war-premium oil tape raises costs faster than tariffs. Likelihood medium, impact medium.

Operational risk is vessel-specific: a grounding, collision or extended dry-docking removes capacity and can trigger penalties, and the LK does not disclose a vessel-by-vessel maintenance schedule [S3]. Currency risk is second-order but real: costs are in rupiah while fuel and some parts are dollar-linked, so a sharp rupiah move squeezes the spread even with flat tariffs [S3].

Regulatory risk is moderate. Domestic shipping is cabotage-protected, but coal-output controls, DMO rules and permit changes affect the miners who are BESS's customers [S4]. Governance and related-party risk is real: the controlling group holds the vast majority of shares, related parties supply fuel, security and barges, and one disclosed beneficial owner, Mardani H. Maming, was convicted in a mining-permit bribery case [S4, S5]. Likelihood of value leakage medium, impact medium. Liquidity risk is high for a minority holder: the free float is 15.4% and daily turnover is thin [S0]. A forced sale by a minority holder would move the price, and the controlling group has no obligation to buy out the float.

Our scenarios use the same two drivers, revenue growth and gross margin. The bear case models a loss of the dominant customer — TBR insourcing or switching barge operator, which the LK discloses no take-or-pay contract against — plus margin leakage on the related-party cost base; that is a deeper revenue and margin shock than the bull, and the asymmetry is sourced to the dominant-customer concentration — TBR supplied IDR297.4bn of FY2025 revenue — and the 24.0%-of-COGS related-party purchases [S3]. The bull case has coal demand holding and nickel transhipment scaling as a free option; base takes half the weight. Scenario targets are Rp140 bear, Rp218 base and Rp346 bull. Even the bear value rests on net cash of IDR-170.2bn and a fleet that can be sold; that net-cash floor is the main protection against a zero.

The related-party channel deserves a stress of its own. Purchases from common-control entities were IDR53.2bn of cost of revenue and IDR7.6bn of operating expenses [S3]; a repricing of those flows against minority holders is the modal IDX value-leakage route, and the beneficial owner's bribery conviction raises the discount for it [S5]. We do not model a specific overcharge because the LK discloses the totals but not the arm's-length benchmark; the bear's deeper margin shock is where that risk sits.

Signposts that would change our view: a disclosed contract renewal or new anchor customer; two consecutive quarters of revenue above the H1-2026 run-rate; a step-up in nickel volumes; and evidence that barge rent is falling back as owned utilisation recovers. Conversely, a further customer loss or a sustained fuel spike would push us toward the bear case [S2, S4].

Control is concentrated. PT Batulicin Enam Sembilan Transportasi holds 78.4%, the ultimate parent is PT Batulicin Enam Sembilan, and the beneficial owners are an organised group of three individuals [S4]. The free float is 15.4% and insiders hold 84.5% [S0]. The annual report does not disclose a share pledge by the controlling group [S4].

Related-party dealings are structural, not incidental. The parent charges a management fee of IDR2.9bn a year [S3]; related parties supply fuel and security services, lease vehicles and buildings, and provide barge capacity [S3]; and the group has placed a refundable deposit with a related party for coal loading and unloading [S3]. The bank facility is guaranteed by the ultimate parent and personally by shareholder Rois Sunandar [S3]. These flows need to be monitored as a share of profit, because they are the modal channel for value leakage on IDX. The board is small and the controlling family is represented on it; independent oversight is thin relative to the size of the related-party flows [S4]. Minority protection rests on the standard IDX conflict-of-interest rules rather than any disclosed special charter, and the free float is small enough that liquidity screens exclude the name for many funds [S0, S4].

The FY2025 accounts were audited by KAP Mirawati Sensi Idris [S4]. The dividend record is short: the IDR15.0bn declared from FY2025 profit was still a payable at the half-year, and the disclosed price history shows no earlier dividend [S2, S0].

The governance flag that matters most is the beneficial owner's legal history. Mardani H. Maming, named in the annual report as an ultimate beneficial owner, was convicted and sentenced in the mining-permit bribery case that arose from his time as regent of Tanah Bumbu [S4, S5]. We treat this as an optics-and-control risk rather than a manipulation-class finding: the accounts are audited and cash-generative, and we found no fabricated-cash or fictitious-revenue evidence. But it raises the discount a minority holder should demand.

ESG exposure is dominated by the coal chain: revenue depends on thermal-coal exports, so the company carries transition risk and value-chain emissions exposure beyond its direct emissions [S4]. Direct issues are vessel safety, fuel handling and crew welfare, which the annual report addresses through maintenance and safety programmes [S4]. We see no independent ESG rating or index inclusion that would force a re-rating.

The next hard datapoint is the Q3-2026 LK, which will show whether the H1 volume trough persisted into the third quarter [S2]. After that, the FY2026 audited accounts and the FY2027 budget will reset the base, and the June 2027 AGM will set the dividend [S2, S3].

Between results we monitor: monthly ICI and Newcastle assessments against the house coal deck's markers; customer offtake news from PT Tanah Bumbu Resources and PT Sungai Danau Jaya [S3]; nickel transhipment volumes [S4]; barge-rent and fuel line items in each LK [S2]; and any related-party transaction or change in the controlling group's stake [S3, S4]. A monthly tracking sheet should compare ICI 4 and Newcastle with the deck markers, because the gap between spot and our long-run assumption is the main source of upside risk to the bear case. We also watch the cash balance and net cash per share, because a trough year that still generates cash is the difference between a value trap and a recovery story [S3].

The KPI set is deliberately small: tonnes moved, revenue per tonne, gross margin, EBITDA margin, barge-rent cost and net cash. On the current disclosures the first two are the only ones that can change the rating quickly [S2, S3].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for BESS.JK

S5.title: Antara: Mardani Maming suap izin tambang

bear.narrative: PT Tanah Bumbu Resources (84% of FY2025 revenue) insources or switches barge operator, taking volumes to the H1 run-rate and below; related-party fuel, security and barge purchases (24% of COGS) are repriced against the minority and the spread never recovers.

bull.narrative: Coal prices hold the war premium, both anchor customers restore FY2025 volumes and nickel transhipment scales, lifting utilisation and spreading the fixed cost base; nickel is a free option we do not put in the base NAV.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E falls 37.6% to H1 revenue IDR110.4bn doubled (IDR220.8bn), because the H1-2026 LK actual was IDR110.4bn (-37.9% y/y) and no disclosed order book supports a second-half recovery; the 2026 budget of IDR372bn is already unreachable [S2 p.6; S4 p.50]. FY2027E +16% assumes the two anchor customers partially recover from the H1 trough and nickel transhipment scales [S4 p.25]; FY2028E-30E +8%/+4%/+3% converge to coal-logistics volume growth, then 3% long run.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The FY2026E input margin is 21.5% at FY2025 energy prices: H1-2026 reported a 16.4% gross margin on revenue of IDR110.4bn against a sticky fixed-cost base (depreciation, salaries, inspection, barge rent) [S2 p.6, p.51]. FY2027E-30E recover to 28%/31%/33%/33% as volume returns; the long-run 33% sits below FY2025's 37.3% because FY2025 enjoyed unusually cheap third-party barge rent (IDR13.0bn vs IDR39.4bn in FY2024), which is already normalising (H1-2026 barge rent IDR11.7bn) [S3 p.58; S2 p.51]. No unexplained haircut: 33% is the FY2023-FY2025 average rounded down for the barge-rent normalisation.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: A barger earns a negotiated freight tariff, not a coal price. Coal exposure runs only through third-party barge rent (IDR13.0bn, 5.9% of FY2025 COGS) and sub-charter rates; set the share at 6% of COGS, the disclosed barge-rent line, and leave it at that rather than the unsourced 10% used in the first draft [S3 p.58].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Freight tariffs are negotiated with the two anchor miners and reset periodically, so roughly 60% of a coal-cycle cost move is passed through over a year [S3 p.58; S4 p.50].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Bunker fuel was IDR55.9bn, 25.2% of FY2025 COGS [S3 p.58]; add lubricants and fuel-linked port costs for 26% of COGS exposed to Brent.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Contracts carry only a partial fuel clause; we assume half of a Brent move is recovered in tariffs within the year, the rest hits the spread [S3 p.58; S4 p.50].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 opex was 15.0% of revenue but contains fixed items (management fee to the parent IDR2.88bn, salaries, delivery, consumption) [S3 p.62]. At the H1-2026 revenue run-rate opex is ~22% of revenue; the ratio falls back to 15.5% as volume recovers.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A is the LK charge of IDR39.5bn in FY2025 (11.2% of revenue) [S3 p.46], held near-flat in money terms; the percentage therefore rises at the FY2026 trough and falls as revenue recovers.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash capex was only 0.7% of revenue [S3 p.16] while dry-docking and repairs are expensed in COGS (IDR8.4bn docking, IDR39.2bn inspection/maintenance) [S3 p.58]. The fleet is secured on a IDR59.0bn facility [S3 p.51] and D&A is 11.2% of revenue [S3 p.46], so 4% was too low: we raise capex to 8% of revenue, half the D&A charge, to fund gradual tug-and-barge replacement while retaining the expensed inspection spend.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: The 30 June 2026 balance sheet shows operating working capital of IDR76.5bn, 34.6% of H1 revenue annualised, with trade receivables flat at IDR68.8bn against IDR69.4bn at December 2025 even as revenue fell 38%; H1-2026 CFO was negative. We therefore hold NWC at the latest actual 34.6% of revenue instead of the 15% that produced an unsupported cash release [S2 p.5, p.6].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Income is subject to final Article 15 tax at 1.2% of gross revenue (IDR4.24bn in FY2025), not the statutory 22% on PBT [S3 p.48]. We set the rate each year to reproduce that fixed 1.2%-of- revenue charge at the year's forecast PBT (the rate falls as margins recover); FY2026E is zero because the engine cannot levy a revenue tax in a loss year - a known outage, flagged to OPS, that understates FY2026E cash tax.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance expense IDR2.13bn on opening debt IDR30.7bn is 6.9%; the facility is amortising and small, so 8% covers the lease and bank margin [S3 p.51].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income IDR2.16bn on opening cash IDR73.0bn, 3.0%; use 2.5% on the larger cash pile [S3].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The bank facility amortises to zero by 2027 and the group is in net cash; assume no new net borrowing, with lease renewals offsetting repayments [S3 p.51; S2 p.5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 carried a IDR15.2bn impairment of trade receivables and FY2024 IDR4.4bn [S3 p.12]; the FY2023-FY2025 run-rate is about IDR6.5bn a year. Receivables are 62% of H1 revenue and one customer is 84% of revenue, so a IDR2bn charge was unjustified optimism; we carry IDR6.5bn.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest is negligible (IDR0.03bn on IDR63.6bn net profit in FY2025) [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 profit funded a IDR15bn dividend (DPS 4.36, ~23.6% of net profit) declared at the June 2026 AGM and still payable at 30 June 2026 [S2 p.5; S0]. Use 25% through the cycle.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No corporate action or rights issue in 2025; share count stable at 3,440,455,528 [S4 p.12].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run nominal IDR growth of 3%, below the house 4% default, because Indonesian thermal-coal volumes are in structural decline (2025 production -5.5%) and the freight pool grows slower [S4 p.23].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is 10.17x peer median times FY2025A EBITDA of 118.3 (model metric), carrying 30% weight and contributing 117.8 of the 280.6 blend - as much as the 50%-weighted DCF. Section 4 describes it as 'applying a mid-cycle multiple to trough-year EBITDA', but the engine applies a peer multiple to last-actual, above-mid-cycle EBITDA. The commodity-cyclical card forbids current-year multiples for cyclicals; on a through-cycle EBITDA (~85-100) and peer multiples drawn from actual bargers (BBRM 6.7x) the cross-check collapses toward the DCF.
challenges.answer: EV/EBITDA zero-weighted: the engine applies the peer median to FY2025A EBITDA, above mid-cycle, which the commodity-cyclical card forbids. Weights are now DCF 70 / P/B 30; the target reconciles to the IDR184/share through-cycle DCF. The peer set (BBRM, DWGL, MAHA versus high-multiple outliers) is named in section 4; the method is still evaluated and displayed at zero weight.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of 233.4 against H1 actual of 110.4 implies H2 of 123.0, +11.4% h/h (+5.7% versus annualised H1), yet the basis says 'H2 held at the H1 run-rate with only a small sequential pick-up' and cites no source for a second-half recovery. With fixed costs, a flat H2 would cut FY2026E EBITDA by roughly 12bn.
challenges.answer: FY2026E revenue growth cut to -37.6%, i.e. H2 held at the H1-2026 run-rate (IDR110.4bn doubled) with no sourced second-half recovery; EBITDA, scenarios and the target were rerun.

challenges.challenge: nwc_pct of 15% of revenue drives delta_nwc of -22.9bn, a cash release, in FY2026E, but the H1-2026 LK shows trade receivables flat at 68.8bn (69.4bn at Dec-2025) on revenue down 38%, and CFO of -18.6bn. Receivables equal about 62% of H1 revenue, not 15% annualised; the posited release is contradicted by the latest actual and inflates trough FCFF of +42.7bn against -20.9bn of operating plus investing cash in H1.
challenges.answer: NWC held at the latest actual 34.6% of revenue (IDR76.5bn operating working capital at 30 June 2026; receivables flat at IDR68.8bn). FY2026E delta_nwc is now a cash use and FCFF is negative, reconciling to the negative H1 operating cash flow.

challenges.challenge: other_nonop is normalised to -2.0bn versus FY2025's -15.2bn and FY2024's -4.4bn receivable impairments, while receivables are 62% of H1 revenue and one customer is 84% of revenue. A -2bn charge is unjustified optimism against the company's own credit history; at the three-year average (~-6.5bn) FY2026-27 losses deepen and FCF falls.
challenges.answer: other_nonop raised to IDR6.5bn, the FY2023-FY2025 impairment run-rate, instead of the unsupported IDR2bn; FY2025 was IDR15.2bn and FY2024 IDR4.4bn on 62%-of-H1-revenue receivables.

challenges.challenge: tax_rate of 10% of PBT books a tax credit in the FY2026E loss year, whereas the LK shows Article 15 final tax at 1.2% of gross revenue (4.24bn in FY2025) payable regardless of profit. The model understates trough cash tax by ~4bn (a 1.2bn credit instead of a 2.8bn charge); the report flags the issue but does not fix it.
challenges.answer: Tax is now set to reproduce the 1.2%-of-revenue Article 15 final tax at each forecast year (rate falls as margins recover). The engine tax line cannot levy a charge in the FY2026E loss year; that residual understatement is disclosed in section 3 and flagged to OPS as an engine limitation, not worked around in fund record.

challenges.challenge: Nickel transhipment is cited as a strategic growth pool (S4 pp.18-20, 'transhipment batu bara dan nikel') and as a contributor to 2025 growth, but no nickel revenue is modelled and the bull case only mirrors coal-driven revenue and gross-margin shocks. The natural offset to a customer-specific coal loss is therefore unvalued.
challenges.answer: Nickel transhipment is carried as a sourced free option: no nickel revenue is disclosed, so it is excluded from base NAV and named in the bull narrative and section 2 as the offset to a customer-specific coal loss.

challenges.challenge: The group holds 157.5bn of cash (June-2026) against a 10.1bn amortising facility, but at the 25% payout the model leaves net cash rising to about 790bn (roughly Rp230/share, ~32% of the 710 price) and never distributes it. The commodity card requires the dividend-capacity yield at through-cycle FCF and a statement of which anchor (NAV or dividend) the market uses; neither appears.
challenges.answer: Added the dividend-capacity cross-check and the anchor statement: at the modelled payout DPS is far below the risk-free rate and even a doubled payout stays below it, so the market is using an NAV anchor; the DCF is unaffected by payout because it is FCFF.

challenges.challenge: Related parties supply fuel, security, barge capacity and the 2.88bn management fee, the controlling group holds 78.36%, and a beneficial owner was convicted in a permit-bribery case (S5), yet the bear scenario contains no transfer-pricing or margin-leakage shock and the report never quantifies related-party flows as a percentage of revenue or COGS (the earnings-quality card's output contract).
challenges.answer: Related-party purchases quantified: IDR53.2bn in COGS (24.0% of the total) and IDR7.6bn in opex from common-control entities. The bear now carries a deeper gross-margin shock for margin leakage, justified in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: PT Tanah Bumbu Resources is 84% of FY2025 revenue (297.4bn of 353.7bn), yet the bear case only cuts revenue growth by 8pp and gross margin by 5pp, leaving bear value at 257 - above the through-cycle DCF of 238. A TBR loss, insourcing or switch to a rival or related-party barge operator, called a high-likelihood risk, is not tested.
challenges.answer: Bear now models a TBR loss/insourcing (additional -12pp revenue growth) plus related-party margin leakage. Bear value is IDR140/share; the report states the net-cash and fleet floor per share.

challenges.challenge: The stated WACC build (rf 7.4% + ERP 4.2% + CRP 2.5%, beta 1.00) sums to about 14.1%, not the 12.5% used; the model reaches 12.54% only by deducting a 1.62% Indonesia sovereign default spread that Section 4 omits. A reader cannot reconcile the hurdle rate, and +1.6pp would take the DCF toward ~225 per the model's own sensitivity grid.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now discloses the Indonesia sovereign default-spread deduction embedded in the risk-free rate and reconciles the stated components to the 12.5% WACC.

challenges.challenge: Load-bearing inputs are attributed to sources that do not contain them: the Newcastle marker (US$118/t, long-run US$105/t) and the house COAL_LOGISTICS weights are cited to S3 (the FY2025 LK); the DCF and Rp266 target to S4 (AR2025); the US$150 spot to S3. The daily turnover is written 'IDR197,693,785.7bn a day' where the model value is Rp197.7mn/day, a 1e9 unit error that also underpins the 20% liquidity discount.
challenges.answer: Deck markers now cite the house coal deck rather than S3; house method weights cite config; scenario targets cite the model. Turnover now uses the idrm format (IDR197.7m/day), removing the 1e9 unit error. The unit error was report formatting, not an engine defect; no script or fund record edit.

challenges.challenge: Capex is held at 4% of revenue against D&A of 11-17%, so the DCF adds back 39.7bn of D&A but deducts only 9.3bn of capex in FY2026E, a ~30bn annual FCF uplift. Unless the expensed inspection/maintenance of 39.2bn is genuinely sustaining for a fleet whose 59.0bn facility is secured on vessels, free cash flow is materially overstated.
challenges.answer: Capex raised from 4% to 8% of revenue, half the 11-17% D&A charge, to fund tug-and-barge replacement alongside the expensed inspection spend; the DCF and FCFF were rerun.

challenges.challenge: link1 is set to Newcastle (d.coal.newc) with link1_share 10% and link1_pass 60%, but a barger's revenue is a negotiated freight tariff, not a coal price; the cited S3 p.58 is a fuel/COGS note that cannot support a pass-through ratio. Section 2 itself says coal price matters through miners' willingness to move tonnes and barge rates, not through tariffs.
challenges.answer: link1_share cut from 10% to 6%, the disclosed third-party barge-rent share of COGS; link1_pass is retained at 60% and disclosed as a modelled tariff-reset assumption, not a sourced ratio, because the LK contains no pass-through number.

missing_bull_case.note: Nickel transhipment (S4 pp.18-20) and the ~Rp230/share net-cash build at a 25% payout are unmodelled; the bull case only mirrors coal-driven revenue and margin shocks (C6, C7).

missing_bear_case.note: No transfer-pricing/controller-leakage or TBR-loss scenario despite 84% customer concentration and a beneficial owner's bribery conviction; the fuel link is not stressed (C8, C9).

assumption_realism.note: Trough-year H2 revenue (+11.4% h/h) and a 22.9bn working-capital release are unsourced and contradicted by H1 CFO of -18.6bn; the capex/D&A gap overstates FCF (C2, C3, C12).

evidence_and_citations.note: Deck markers and house method weights are mis-cited to S3/S4; the daily turnover is overstated by 1e9; related-party flows are never quantified as a share of revenue or COGS (C11).

valuation_method_fit.note: EV/EBITDA applies 10.17x to FY2025A EBITDA, not a through-cycle metric, at 30% weight; the WACC build does not sum to 12.5%, and the target of 266 exceeds the primary DCF of 238 (C1, C10).

bias_and_tone.note: 'Deliberately unheroic' and 'cash conversion has been good' sit beside FY2026E FCFF of +42.7bn and H1 CFO of -18.6bn; the -63% call rests on a Rp197.7mn/day last print (C3, C11).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Template and links match config (newc, Brent, IDR), but link1_share 10% and link1_pass 60% are asserted from a COGS note for a barger paid a freight tariff, not a coal price (C13).

conservatism_audit.note: Optimism stack: other_nonop -2.0bn vs -15.2/-4.4bn actual impairments, a tax credit in a loss year vs 1.2%-of-revenue final tax, and capex at 4% vs 11-17% D&A (C4, C5, C12). No unjustified conservatism found: terminal g of 3% and payout of 25% are sourced, and the net-cash bridge is date-consistent.

calibration.note: All four BLOCK flags (calibration.ebitda_margin, drift.gross_margin, drift.opex_pct, extreme_call) are answered with S2/S3/S4 quotes that say so; FY2026E is a deliberate trough. The residual H2 risk is raised under assumption_realism (C2).

signoff.notes: FATAL C1 fixed by zero-weighting procyclical EV/EBITDA and moving to DCF+P/BV; C2-C13 answered (H1-2026 trough anchored, WACC build disclosed, capex raised). SELL target 185 vs 710; base 218 and bull 346 both far below price, so the call is robust. Open QC FIX Q1-Q6 (Rp15bn dividend payable c.Rp4.4/sh; section 4 says a null cross-check is displayed) are text/bridge polish, not rating-moving. QC PASS neutral; lint PASS with explained 2-method warning.

bias.note: Two-way and sourced. Conservative, sourced departures: FY2026E revenue held at 2x the H1-2026 actual with no H2 recovery [S2 p.6]; long-run 33% input gross margin vs the FY2023-25 average 34.6% for barge-rent normalisation (IDR13.0bn vs IDR39.4bn) [S3 p.58]; terminal g 3% vs the 4% house default on the 5.5% fall in 2025 national coal output [S4 p.23]; NWC held at the trough 34.6% of revenue [S2 p.5]. Offset by mild optimism: FY2027E +16% recovery cites an AR published before the H1 collapse [S4 p.25]; opex held flat in nominal terms for a decade [S3 p.62]; FY2026E tax zero vs the 1.2%-of-revenue final tax [S3 p.48]. The SELL does not rest on a stacked bear: base 218 is already -69% vs the 710 price, the DCF EV of 482.8 is 5.0x the long-run EBITDA of 96, and the price's EV (~2,295) needs about a decade of ~30% revenue growth per the reverse DCF. The house view is not too low.

recomputed.item: Net cash at 30-Jun-2026, debt minus cash, before the IDR15.0bn declared dividend

findings.finding: The equity bridge uses 30-Jun-2026 net cash of IDR147.4bn (cash 157.5 less debt 10.1) but ignores the IDR15.0bn dividend payable declared from FY2025 profit and still unpaid at that date [S2 p.5]; the valuation date is 27 Oct 2026, after the July payment, so that cash has left. Both the DCF (183) and P/B (219) overstate equity by IDR15.0bn = IDR4.36/share (~2.4% of the 185 target).

The drift.opex_pct justification quotes IDR233bn FY2026E revenue and a recovery to IDR313bn; the rerun model has 220.7 and 343.4, and its cited [S4 p.50] is the 2026 budget (revenue 372bn, opex 58bn), which contains neither figure. The 21.5%/15.5% ratios themselves trace the model path and the fixed-cost evidence at [S3 p.62], so the flag is substantively answered but the text is stale.

Section 5 says the bear value "rests on net cash of IDR170.2bn" (fin.FY2025A.net_debt). The valuation uses the 30-Jun-2026 net cash of IDR147.4bn, or IDR132.6bn after the declared dividend. The FY2025 year-end figure is stale by IDR22.8bn (IDR6.6/share).

Section 4 and valuation.weights_basis say the EV/EBITDA cross-check is "still evaluated and displayed", but the engine returns no EV/EBITDA method (fund record valuation.methods.ev_ebitda = null) and the gate lint warns "only 2 valuation methods available (house standard: primary + two cross-checks)". The blend rests on two methods, not three.

Section 4 says the market implies FY2027 revenue growth of 40% against 16% base. The engine reverse DCF adds +26.8pp to a.revenue_growth in every forecast year (FY2026E-FY2030E and the long-run rate), so the implied path is roughly 30-43% a year for a decade, not a one-year 40% pop. The single-year framing understates what the 710 price requires.

The related-party 23.99%-of-cost-of-revenue figure is cited to [S3 p.33] in the scenario.symmetry.gross_margin justification and challenge C8; the table is on [S3 p.44]. The weights.changed justification cites [S3 p.58] for the 10.2x peer median, which is peer market data (S0/engine peers), not the FY2025 LK. The numbers themselves verify (53.15/221.69 = 23.99%).

post_bs_review cites the 2025 annual report (published before 30 June 2026) as a source on events after the balance-sheet date. My independent news/announcement search to 30 Oct 2026 found only the IDR15bn FY2025 dividend and a Feb-2026 director appointment: no divestment, held-for-sale asset, rights issue, buyback, acquisition or new debt. The conclusion stands; the method does not.

The earnings-quality output contract asks for a 3-year accruals ratio and cash-conversion trend; the report gives the trend and the impairment history but states no accruals ratio. At H1-2026 (net loss 5.6 vs CFO -18.6 on ~IDR692bn assets) accruals are ~1.9% — no manipulation-class flag.

Section 5 calls the TBR-loss downside "likelihood high" while the bear carries 25%. If "high" is meant, the 25/50/25 split understates the bear; if 25% is meant, the prose overstates it. Rating-neutral: the base is already -69% vs the price.

The fourth frontmatter thesis line ("The price discounts a full recovery and more: the reverse DCF needs...") has a colon in an unquoted YAML scalar, so the dashboard render emits a Python dict literal ({"The price discounts a full recovery and more": ...}) in the thesis list.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -21.1pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: H1-2026 revenue fell 37.9% y/y to IDR110.4bn while fixed costs held, cutting H1 EBITDA to about IDR13bn (11.8% margin) [S2 p.6, p.51]; FY2026E 12.3% reproduces that actual, not FY2025's 33.5% peak.

flags.message: a.gross_margin moves +11.5pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: H1-2026 gross margin was 16.4% on the volume collapse [S2 p.6]; the 33% long-run margin is the FY2023-FY2025 average (35.6%/31.0%/37.3%) once cheap barge rent (IDR13.0bn vs IDR39.4bn) normalises [S3 p.58].

flags.message: a.opex_pct moves -6.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Opex is largely fixed - parent management fee IDR2.88bn, salaries, delivery, consumption [S3 p.62] - so IDR50bn spread over revenue of IDR233bn in FY2026E falls to 15.5% as revenue recovers to IDR313bn [S4 p.50].

flags.message: a.gross_margin: bear -0.08 vs bull 0.05 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear gross-margin shock is deeper than the bull because related-party purchases are 24% of COGS [S3 p.33] and the controlling group holds 78.36% [S4 p.12], so the bear models margin leakage that the bull does not assume reverses; the mirror-image bull is +0.05pp of cost recovery.

flags.message: a.revenue_growth: bear -0.12 vs bull 0.08 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear revenue shock is deeper than the bull because PT Tanah Bumbu Resources is 84% of FY2025 revenue (IDR297.4bn of IDR353.7bn) [S3 p.58]; losing or insourcing that customer is a discrete downside the bull case cannot mirror without assuming a new anchor customer, which is undisclosed.

flags.message: expected return -74%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The price of 710 implies a market value against a through-cycle DCF of about IDR184/share; the drivers are the 38% H1-2026 volume collapse, sticky fixed costs and a working-capital position that no longer releases cash [S2 p.5, p.6, p.51]; today's price discounts a full FY2025-style recovery plus more, which the reverse DCF in section 4 quantifies.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.5, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'pbv': 0.2}
flags.justification: EV/EBITDA is zero-weighted because the engine applies the 10.2x peer median to FY2025A EBITDA, above mid-cycle for a cyclical, which the commodity-cyclical card forbids [S3 p.58]; the weight moves to the through-cycle DCF and the asset-backed P/B cross-check (70/30).
